transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

I guess… I came in because I just feel wound up most of the day. Like my body is bracing for something, even when nothing is happening. I’ll be sitting at my computer, just doing normal work, and I notice I’m all tense for no real reason. And then even after dinner, when I’m supposed to be relaxing, it’s like I can’t quite settle. It’s hard to explain—I keep thinking maybe it’s just how I am, but it’s been bothering me.
Is there one particular situation or thing that tends to set off this tense, wound-up feeling?

Not really one thing, no. It’s more like it just… shows up. Like I’ll be sitting at my computer doing regular work, nothing dramatic happening, and I notice my shoulders are up and I’m all braced like I’m waiting for bad news or something. And then later after dinner, when I should be able to just sit and watch something, it’s still there.

I mean, sometimes I wonder if it’s the computer work itself because I’ve been doing that forever, and the chair at my desk is probably terrible—I keep meaning to replace it—but it doesn’t feel like just that. It’s more like my body is wound up most of the day, even when there isn’t a clear reason.
Have you had sudden episodes where intense fear or physical panic comes on all at once?

I’m not sure I’d call it sudden intense fear, exactly. I mean, I’ve had times where I realize I’m really tense, but it’s not like—at least I don’t think—it comes crashing in all at once.

Though sometimes I wonder if I’m just so used to being wound up that I wouldn’t notice the difference. My sister once described something she had in a grocery store, and that sounded very dramatic, like she thought she had to leave immediately, and I remember thinking, “Oh, I don’t think that’s me.” But… no, I can’t really point to episodes like that.
Did this start after a specific stressful life event?

I think so, yes… or at least it lines up with one. It’s been about thirteen months now, since my sister in Arecibo started needing a lot more help from the family.

And, I mean, it’s not like one dramatic day where everything changed. It was more gradual—phone calls, figuring things out, people having opinions about who should do what. My family can turn one small decision into a whole committee meeting, you know? But that’s around when I noticed this becoming more constant.
Has this wound-up feeling been present for more than six months?

Yes, definitely more than six months. It’s been about thirteen months, I think—since my sister in Arecibo started needing a lot more help from everyone. That’s sort of when it became this constant background thing. I remember because it was around the time we were all on the phone so much, and my cousin kept saying we needed a spreadsheet for who was doing what, which honestly was not a bad idea, but… yes. More than six months.
Do you find that the worrying feels hard to control?

Yes… I’d say it is hard to control. I’ll tell myself, “Daniela, enough, focus on this report,” and I really mean to, but then one little thought turns into five other things.

Like I’ll think, “Let me just check that message,” and then I’m replaying what could go wrong, or whether I missed something, and suddenly half an hour has gone by. It’s not dramatic, exactly, but it kind of pulls me away before I notice.
Have you been feeling down or depressed much of the time?

I’m not sure I’d call it depressed, exactly. I mean, I have moments where I feel low, like anyone, especially when there’s too much going on—but “much of the time”… I don’t know. I haven’t really been keeping track of it that way.

When you say depressed, do you mean like sad all day, or more like not interested in anything? Because those feel a little different to me.
Have you been feeling sad or down most days?

Most days… I don’t think so? I mean, I can feel down here and there, like if the day gets away from me or I’m tired, but I wouldn’t say I’m sad most days.

Although sometimes I wonder if I’m just used to pushing through things. My mother used to say, “You don’t have time to fall apart,” which—probably not the healthiest family motto. But no, if you’re asking sad most days, I don’t think that’s really it.
Do you feel your anxiety is stronger than the situation with your sister would reasonably call for?

Yes… probably. I mean, I do worry about my sister in Arecibo, and some of that makes sense, but it doesn’t stay just there. My mind kind of hops from that to whether I missed something at the office, then to my husband driving home, then church things I said I’d help with, bills… it’s like I start preparing for problems that haven’t even happened.

And then I’ll tell myself, “Okay, but what can you actually do right now?”—because my father used to say that, he was very practical—but I still keep going through all the possibilities anyway. So yes, I guess it does feel bigger than the situation calls for.
Do you worry about many different parts of your life, not just your sister’s situation?

Yes, it’s not just my sister. It sort of starts there sometimes, because she’s in Arecibo and I get concerned, but then my mind jumps all over. Like, did I miss something at the office, is my husband okay driving home, did I forget I said I’d help with something at church, are the bills handled… one thing leads to another.

I’ll be making coffee or trying to answer an email, and suddenly I’m planning for three problems that haven’t even happened. It’s like my brain wants to be ready for everything, even when there’s nothing I can actually do right then.
Has this anxiety been making it hard for you to function in your daily life?

A little, yes. I’m still functioning—I mean, I get my work done, I show up for my family, I go to church and do what I said I’d do. So it’s not like everything has fallen apart.

But things take me longer than they used to. Reports at work, especially, I’ll keep checking them over and over, and then I’m behind on the next thing. My husband teases me that I “review the review,” which—well, he’s not wrong.

And I’ve noticed I can sound short with people. Not because I mean to. I’ll be thinking about five things at once, and then someone asks me something simple and I answer too sharply. I’ve had to apologize for that, especially with people I really care about. So… yes, it’s affecting things, just not in a dramatic way.
Have you been having trouble sleeping?

Yes… somewhat. I usually do fall asleep eventually, so it’s not like I’m lying there the whole night. But a lot of nights I wake up around three or four in the morning, and then my brain just starts.

It’ll be something like my sister’s next appointment, or then suddenly I’m thinking about a server issue at work—my job is on computers, so those things have a way of following me home, even though they really shouldn’t. And then once I’m awake, it’s hard to feel like I really went back into restful sleep.

Even if I technically got enough hours, I’ll get up feeling like I didn’t really rest. Like I slept, but I didn’t… recover, if that makes sense.
If the situation with your sister were resolved, do you think this anxiety would still be there?

Yes… I think it would still be there. Maybe it would be quieter, because my sister being in Arecibo is definitely one of the big things my mind grabs onto. But it’s not only that.

If it wasn’t her appointment or whether she’s okay, it would be something at the office—like did I miss an email, did I make some mistake in a report—or my husband driving home, or something I promised to do at church. Even bills, little things that probably are fine. My mind just sort of moves down the list and then makes a second list, if that makes sense.

I keep catching myself preparing for problems that haven’t happened. Like I’m rehearsing emergencies. So yes, I think even if her situation got better, my brain would probably just find the next thing to worry over.
Do you often feel easily fatigued?

I’m not sure I’d say “easily” fatigued. I mean, I do get tired, but… I’m 57, I work on a computer all day, and sometimes I think staring at screens makes anybody feel drained.

Some days I’ll sit down after dinner and think, oh, I could just stay right here. But then there are other days I’m fine, I can do what needs doing. So I don’t know if it’s fatigue in the way you mean, or just normal tiredness. My husband would probably say I keep going even when I should stop, but he says that about everything, honestly.
Before your sister started needing more help, were you already someone who worried this much about lots of different things?

Not really this much, no. I mean, I’ve always been the kind of person who likes to know what the plan is—my husband says I make lists for my lists, which… he’s not wrong. But this level of worrying about everything, that’s been more recent.

I’d say it started about thirteen months ago, when my sister in Arecibo began needing a lot more help from the family. That sort of kicked it into a higher gear, and then it started spreading into other things too.
Has your anxiety kept going even during times when things with your sister were relatively calm?

Yes, it has. I mean, there have been weeks where my sister’s situation wasn’t actively on fire, you know—no appointment that day, no urgent call from Arecibo—and I’d think, okay, maybe I’ll relax a little.

But then my mind just… shifts over. Like, did I miss something at work, did I forget an email, is my husband home yet, did I say I’d help with something at church, are the bills all set. It’s almost like once one thing quiets down, another thing raises its hand.

I find myself planning for problems that haven’t happened yet, which sounds silly when I say it out loud, but in the moment it feels like I’m being responsible. So yes, even when things with her are calmer, the worrying doesn’t really stop.
If your sister had not started needing more help, do you think this level of anxiety would have begun anyway?

I don’t think so… or at least, not at this level. I’ve always been a planner, like I said, but it really started about thirteen months ago, when my sister in Arecibo began needing much more help from the family.

I mean, maybe I would’ve found something else to fuss over—my husband says I can turn a grocery list into a project—but this feels different. It’s like that situation opened the door, and then the worrying just stayed.
Has this level of anxiety lasted longer than six months after your sister first started needing more help?

Yes—definitely longer than six months. It’s been about thirteen months now, since my sister in Arecibo started needing a lot more help from the family.

I remember because it was around when we were trying to coordinate who could go when, and then I had this whole calendar situation with color-coding—my husband teased me about it—but yes, the short answer is it’s been over a year.
Do you feel most of your anxiety is specifically about your sister’s situation?

Not only my sister, no. She’s definitely a big part of it, especially with her being in Arecibo and trying to keep track of what’s going on from here, but it doesn’t stay there.

My mind kind of hops around. I’ll be worrying about her, and then suddenly I’m thinking, wait, did I miss something at the office? Or if my husband is driving home, I start wondering if he’s okay. Then I remember something at church I may have said yes to, or I start thinking about bills.

It’s like I’m always preparing for the next problem, even if nothing has actually happened yet. So… my sister may have started it, but most of the anxiety isn’t only about her anymore.
Have there been any periods since this started when the family situation with your sister was truly resolved?

Not really, no. I mean, there were maybe little stretches where things seemed calmer, and I’d think, okay, maybe we’ve got a handle on this—but then something else would come up, or I’d start wondering if we’d missed something.

It’s been going on about thirteen months now, since my sister in Arecibo started needing a lot more help from the family. And honestly, with family things, “resolved” is such a funny word… my cousin always says everything is temporary, especially when relatives are involved. But no, I wouldn’t say it was ever truly resolved in that time.

But then my mind just… shifts over. Like, did I miss something at work, did I forget an email, is my husband home yet, did I say I’d help with something at church, are the bills all set. It’s almost like once one thing quiets down, another thing raises its hand.

I find myself planning for problems that haven’t happened yet, which sounds silly when I say it out loud, but in the moment it feels like I’m being responsible. So yes, even when things with her are calmer, the worrying doesn’t really stop.
